title: Method: Earth terrain that matches the lunar south-pole base regions

sections.title: Two decisions and how they were made
paragraphs: Which elevation model feeds the ranking. The rule was written before the numbers existed (pipeline.score.dem_policy_from_rule): NASADEM, with MODIS land cover, is primary for the tiles it covers (56 S to 60 N) if the per-tile share of candidate cells from the two inputs has a Spearman correlation of at least 0.90 and at least 35 of the top 50 tiles are shared; otherwise Copernicus stays primary and NASADEM is a cross-check. Above 60 N and below 56 S Copernicus is the only source either way. Outcome: not met. On 618 tiles and 1.12 million common cells the Spearman correlation is 0.637 and 21 of the top 50 tiles are shared (data/validation/nasadem_vs_copdem.json, docs/figures/nasadem_vs_copdem.png). Copernicus is the elevation model of the ranking; NASADEM is the cross-check. What the cross-check shows: slopes and roughness from 400 m up are the same in both models (correlation 0.99 and above, median ratio within 3%), roughness at 200 m scatters, and closed depressions do not agree (correlation 0.76; NASADEM has small depressions almost everywhere). Through the depression features the list of candidate cells depends on the elevation model: on the 618 common tiles, 33,911 candidate cells with Copernicus, 2,996 with NASADEM, 2,237 in common (candidates.esa, candidates.nasa, candidate_cells_shared_esa_nasa; the whole scan has 63,618).

Which lunar target and which ranking key. Default target: the seven candidate regions pooled; ranking key: best 15 km window. The J18 comparison did not distinguish the pooled target from the 160 km polar window: known analog sites were recovered similarly (15 of 35 above the base rate with a median enrichment of 0.91, against 16 of 35 and 0.97), and six well-known reference tiles rank somewhat worse under the pooled target (Atacama core 40th against 18th of about 2,060 tiles, Mauna Loa 49th against 48th). The pooled target is kept because the challenge asks for analogs of the base locations, and those regions are steeper than the polar average (median slope at 240 m 7.0 deg against 5.1 deg): this is a choice of definition, not a measured improvement. Every site also carries its score against each single region and against the polar window. The best-window key replaces total area because total area rewarded sheer size: with it, sand seas held the first four ranks.

sections.title: What the validation says
paragraphs: The estimator reproduces NASA's lunar slope map (step 4).

Around the 22 catalogued lunar analogs (tagged lunar or both; Mars-only entries are not tested), median enrichment was 1.02, versus 0.39 for random circles (5th to 95th percentile: 0.12 to 0.91). Fourteen of 500 random repeats reached the observed median. The typical known lunar site had about the scan-wide bare-cell share of lunar-like ground. At one-degree tile scale, the corrected recovery AUC of 0.531 was consistent with chance. Validation
Laser profiles of ICESat-2 over eight sites give 0.43 to 1.16 times the grid slope at 240 m (median 0.87); the three lowest are lava fields, and the laser samples a 20 km box, not the site outline.
The dune-field flag removes the sand seas from the top 50 and also flags part of Devon Island, a real analog.

A second elevation model (NASADEM, NASA) gives the same slopes and a different set of candidate cells: three quarters of its candidates are also candidates with Copernicus, but only 7% of the Copernicus candidates survive. The list of candidate cells depends on the elevation model; the top of the ranking depends most on the land-cover mask (3 of the top 30 survive the strict mask) and on the feature set (5 of the top 30 survive leaving roughness out), and little on the lunar sample (ranks 1 to 9 move by at most 4 places).

In short: the score is consistent with chance at tile scale (AUC 0.531) and borderline at site scale (2.8% of random runs reach the known sites' median, random.share_of_random_runs_with_median_at_least_ours). It is a screen for terrain shape, not a detector of analogs.

Only 4 of the 44 lunar known analogs were chosen for their terrain (J31, data/reference/known_analogs_selected_for.csv): 2 eligible tiles and 2 tested circles, too few to test (effectiveness.json recovery.by_selected_for.terrain, enrichment.json by_selected_for.terrain). The method may therefore claim that the terrain statistics of the listed sites fall inside the lunar range, not that it finds analog terrain.

sections.title: Limits
paragraphs: Shape of the terrain at 240 m to 1.6 km only: no rocks, no regolith, no vacuum, no low sun. A 30 m surface model sees vegetation and smooths small craters. The top of the ranking is Arctic plateau terrain (16 of the top 30 sites are one landform, the Putorana Plateau) and its "bare ground" is mostly moss-and-lichen tundra, because the land-cover class "moss and lichen" counts as bare (see "Mask choice" below: under a mask without it, 3 of the top 30 remain); read it with the review in data/sites/top30_review.csv (26 of 30 not artefacts, 4 unsure under cloud). Closed depressions on Earth are often lakes and thermokarst; the top-30 sites have a depression share of zero in the median cell, so that is not what ranks them. The coldest monthly night mean among the 60 top sites is 235 K; the lunar regions have annual means of 51 to 141 K. Exact top sites move with the grid (6 of 10 survive a half-cell shift on the 78-tile test); regions are stable. Nothing here is called a discovery. The literature checks (one to four English web searches per site row, and the J35 second pass of analog catalogues, OpenAlex and Russian searches) found, for the default top 30, 2 sites in known analog regions, 10 in regions named as Mars analogs and 18 "not found in the analog catalogues and searches listed here"; for the strict top 30, 9, 12 and 9 (novelty of data/sites/ranking.csv and of the strict ranking, ranks 1 to 30; docs/NOVELTY.md). Every "mentioned" is a Mars-analog statement. These verdicts are an SI model's; a person has not checked them. Ranking window on narrow polar tiles (J43): until 15 Nov the key fell back to the whole site on tiles with fewer than 8 columns, which put three southern Peary Land sites at ranks 1, 3 and 4; with the window clipped to the tile they rank 14, 16 and 20 and the top-30 set is unchanged (data/validation/window_rule/window_rule.json, masks.default). The cell area used for the key is cell_m² (3.92 km²) on every tile, although cells near 82 N are about 1.99 km wide.

Mask choice (J33, full run on all 2,060 tiles): the default mask counts WorldCover class 100 "moss and lichen" as bare, so the top of the default ranking is mostly moss-and-lichen tundra. With class 60 only (python -m pipeline.sites --bare-col bare_strict, a variant; the default is unchanged) 3 of the default top 30 and 16 of the top 100 have a strict site within 3 km, candidate cells fall from 63,618 to 35,875 and sites from 3,175 to 1,561, and the strict top 30 is Atacama and Puna (13), the western Tibetan Plateau (8), southern Peru and Arica (4), the Hazen Plateau and northern Ellesmere (3) and Mauna Loa (1) (data/validation/landcover_sensitivity.json, full_run.overlap, full_run.candidate_cells, full_run.sites, full_run.regions_top30). Both rankings are presented; the strict one is the conservative reading (VALIDATION.md). The strict leaders are high, dry deserts and are warmer, not closer to lunar temperatures: median 12-month MODIS day surface temperature of the top 30 is 296 K against 261 K for the default top 30, and the night mean is about 150 K above the Diviner annual mean of the best-matching lunar region in both rankings (149 K strict, 146 K default; data/validation/landcover_sensitivity/context_comparison.json, groups.{default,strict}.modis_lst_day_mean_k.median, night_minus_diviner_mean_k.median). Its top 30 had the image review (NASA Worldview MODIS/VIIRS and HLS 30 m: 28 no, 2 unsure, 0 artefacts; data/validation/landcover_sensitivity/top30_strict_review.csv) and the literature check of J40 (docs/NOVELTY.md section 7). *DECISION FOR THE TEAM: which of the two rankings is the headline (issue #11).*
